The piston has to bear the pressure produced by the maximum load resting on it.
\(p = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{mg}{A} = \dfrac{2000 \times 9.8}{2.25 \times 10^{-2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{1.96 \times 10^{4}}{2.25 \times 10^{-2}} = 8.711 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^2 = 0.8711 \times 10^{6}\) N/m\(^2\).
The result is not sensitive to the value taken for \(g\): with \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\) it is \(8.72 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^2\), still the same option. The three remaining values are out by factors of about 6.7, 18 and 266, so exactly one option fits.

For capillary rise, \(h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\). The same liquid is used in both tubes, so \(T\), \(\theta\) and \(\rho\) are the same and \(h \propto \dfrac{1}{r}\) — the narrower tube gives the greater rise.
\(\dfrac{h_1}{h_2} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \dfrac{0.6}{0.3} = \dfrac{2}{1}\)
So the ratio is \(2 : 1\). The printed alternative \(1 : 2\) is the same ratio inverted and would follow from \(h \propto r\); \(1 : 4\) and \(4 : 1\) are the \(r^2\) ratios and would follow from a wrong power of \(r\). Only \(2 : 1\) survives.

The energy stored is the surface energy, \(E = T \times \) (surface area). A soap **bubble** has TWO free surfaces (inner and outer), so its area is \(2 \times 4\pi r^2 = 8\pi r^2\).
Diameter 6 cm \(\Rightarrow r = 3\) cm \(= 0.03\) m.
\(E = 0.04 \times 8\pi (0.03)^2 = 0.04 \times 2.262 \times 10^{-2} = 9.05 \times 10^{-4}\) J \(\approx 0.9 \times 10^{-3}\) J.
Counting only one surface would give \(4.52 \times 10^{-4}\) J, half as much — that is the trap the question is set to catch. Note it falls between the printed \(0.4 \times 10^{-3}\) J and \(0.5 \times 10^{-3}\) J and matches neither cleanly, whereas the two-surface value sits squarely on \(0.9 \times 10^{-3}\) J. The remaining alternative, \(0.7 \times 10^{-3}\) J, follows from no defensible reading.

The terminal velocity of a sphere falling through a viscous medium is
\(v = \dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}\), so for hail stones of the same material falling through the same air, \(v \propto r^2\).
\(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{16}\)
So the ratio is \(1 : 16\). The printed \(1 : 2\) would follow from \(v \propto \sqrt{r}\) and \(1 : 8\) from \(v \propto r^{3/2}\); neither power is Stokes' law, and \(1 : 12\) is no power of \(r\) at all. Only \(1 : 16\) fits.

Bernoulli's equation is obtained in this chapter by applying the work-energy theorem to a fluid element: the net work done by the pressure of the surrounding fluid equals the change in kinetic energy plus the change in gravitational potential energy, \(W = \Delta K.E. + \Delta P.E.\) The chapter states it plainly — Bernoulli's principle is consistent with the principle of conservation of **energy**.
Mass is indeed conserved in the flow, but that is the content of the *equation of continuity* \((Av = \) constant\()\), a separate result — so *mass* is the intended distractor here. Linear momentum is not conserved (the surrounding fluid exerts pressure forces on the element), and angular momentum plays no part in the derivation.
